paras: The lynching of Jim Robinson was the hanging of a Black man at Shaw, Mississippi, on the night of Tuesday, August 26, 1890. Robinson had been accused of outraging the 8-year-old daughter of Henry Meyers near Shaw earlier that week. The killing drew only brief notice in two Mississippi weeklies, both of which treated the accusation as established fact.

According to the Greenville Times, Robinson was accused of outraging the young daughter of Henry Meyers near Shaw in the last week of August. He was hanged on the following Tuesday night, August 26. Neither account describes who hanged him, how many took part, whether he had been arrested beforehand, or where exactly the hanging took place.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Greenville Times reported the hanging on August 30 in a one-sentence editorial paragraph, printed among short items on politics and local amusements. It called Robinson "the negro brute" and wrote that he "kicked at the United States from the end of a piece of hemp," presenting the accusation without qualification or source. The paper did not use the word "lynched" or mention a mob.

A week later, on September 5, the Southern Herald of Liberty, Mississippi, carried a single line among its "Editorial Items" stating that "a negro ravisher was lynched at Shaw." That brief gave the date but not Robinson's name, and like the Greenville Times it treated the charge as proven. No Black-press account of the hanging appears in the coverage from August and September 1890.

reader.title: Lynching of Jim Robinson
bases: A Black man accused of rape was hanged without any reported legal process, and a later brief called it a lynching (A1, A2).
Robinson was hanged after an accusation of outraging a child (A1) and the Southern Herald called it a lynching (A2), but neither paper describes the people who hanged him or their number.

Two Mississippi papers agree on a hanging at Shaw of a Black man accused of rape in the last week of August (A1, A2); the Southern Herald brief adds the date and the word 'lynched', though it may derive from exchanges rather than independent reporting.

accounts.label: Greenville Times editorial paragraph
accounts.gist: Named Robinson, called him a 'negro brute' who outraged Henry Meyers's 8-year-old daughter near Shaw, and said he was hanged last Tuesday night.

accounts.label: Southern Herald brief
accounts.gist: Reported in one line that a 'negro ravisher' was lynched at Shaw on August 26, without names.

framing.detail: The Greenville Times called Robinson a 'negro brute', asserted the outrage as fact, and described the hanging with the joke that he 'kicked at the United States from the end of a piece of hemp'.
The Southern Herald ran a bare one-line item among miscellaneous news, using 'negro ravisher' and treating the accusation as established.
